groups.title: Service boundaries
groups.mechanism: A service boundary groups a cohesive business capability with ownership of its data and operational contract. Deployment independence is an outcome, not merely a separate process.
groups.tradeOff: Fine-grained splitting increases network, coordination and ownership costs.
groups.verify: Trace one business change and count the teams, deployments and synchronous calls it requires.

questions.question: What defines a microservice?
questions.answer: An independently deployable service owning a focused capability and explicit contracts, rather than simply a small HTTP application.

questions.question: When is a modular monolith preferable?
questions.answer: When independent scaling or ownership does not justify distributed coordination, and strong module boundaries can preserve clarity in one deployment.

questions.question: How does bounded context help service design?
questions.answer: It identifies where terminology and business rules have consistent meaning, guiding boundaries and preventing accidental shared domain assumptions.

questions.question: Why is splitting services by database table often ineffective?
questions.answer: Business operations can span many tables, creating chatty calls and coordinated changes instead of cohesive ownership.

questions.question: How would you evaluate an existing service boundary?
questions.answer: Measure change coupling, data ownership, latency and failure dependencies, then consider merging or splitting based on operational and domain evidence.

groups.title: Data ownership
groups.mechanism: Owning a database means controlling its schema and access contract, even when physical infrastructure is shared. Direct cross-service writes bypass that authority.
groups.tradeOff: Local autonomy increases the need for explicit data synchronization and reporting patterns.
groups.verify: Change a schema while exercising every known consumer and inspect unauthorized direct access.

questions.question: Why should a service own its data?
questions.answer: To maintain its invariants and evolve its schema without external writers silently violating business rules or requiring coordinated releases.

questions.question: When is a shared physical database acceptable?
questions.answer: When ownership, permissions and schemas preserve service boundaries and the operational trade-off is deliberate rather than accidental coupling.

questions.question: How can one service obtain another service's data?
questions.answer: Through an explicit API, published event or managed replicated view with defined freshness and compatibility semantics.

questions.question: Why are cross-service database joins risky?
questions.answer: They couple schemas, availability and performance across owners, often bypassing authorization and making independent deployment difficult.

questions.question: How would you support cross-service reporting?
questions.answer: Build an explicit read model or analytical pipeline with provenance, reconciliation and freshness guarantees instead of unrestricted operational-table access.

groups.title: API contracts
groups.mechanism: An API contract includes meanings, errors, ordering, limits and compatibility, not just a schema. Clients need stable ways to interpret absence and uncertain outcomes.
groups.tradeOff: Strict contracts improve reliability but require migration and versioning discipline.
groups.verify: Replay historical requests and malformed inputs against both old and new implementations.

questions.question: What makes an API backward compatible?
questions.answer: Existing supported clients can continue obtaining documented behavior, including field meaning, defaults, statuses and error recovery.

questions.question: When should an API be versioned explicitly?
questions.answer: When a behavioral or representation change cannot be introduced compatibly within the existing contract and consumer migration is necessary.

questions.question: How does pagination become part of the contract?
questions.answer: Ordering, cursor validity, duplicate handling and concurrent changes determine which records clients observe across pages.

questions.question: Why can adding a required field break existing clients?
questions.answer: Older clients omit it, so validation or default semantics change. Use tolerant evolution or an explicit new contract.

questions.question: How would you design a safe partial update API?
questions.answer: Distinguish omitted, null and supplied values, validate authorization per field and use version conditions to avoid silently overwriting concurrent changes.

groups.title: Synchronous call chains
groups.mechanism: Each synchronous hop consumes latency budget and couples availability. Parallelism changes coordination and downstream load rather than removing dependency risk.
groups.tradeOff: Simple request-response flows can become fragile when critical paths grow long.
groups.verify: Inject latency into each hop and measure total deadline consumption plus fallback behavior.

questions.question: When is synchronous communication appropriate?
questions.answer: When the caller needs a timely response from another capability and the latency, availability and failure coupling are acceptable.

questions.question: What is the risk of a long synchronous service chain?
questions.answer: Its response depends on many components and accumulated waits, so one slow dependency can exhaust upstream deadlines.

questions.question: How should deadlines propagate across services?
questions.answer: Carry or calculate remaining budget and allocate time to acquisition, work and response handling without restarting a full timeout at every hop.

questions.question: Why can parallel fan-out worsen an outage?
questions.answer: It multiplies simultaneous downstream requests and retained work, especially when callers retry after one branch fails.

questions.question: How would you design a bounded aggregation endpoint?
questions.answer: Limit fan-out and pending work, define required versus optional branches, apply shared deadlines and return truthful partial or unavailable outcomes.

groups.title: Idempotency
groups.mechanism: Idempotency ties repeated requests to one logical operation. Durable state must handle concurrent duplicates and unknown outcomes, not merely remember recent successes.
groups.tradeOff: Deduplication storage and retention cost are part of the operation contract.
groups.verify: Submit the same key concurrently and retry after a committed effect whose response was lost.

questions.question: What is an idempotent operation?
questions.answer: Repeating the same logical operation has the promised effect no more than intended, even if requests or delivery occur multiple times.

questions.question: When should an API require an idempotency key?
questions.answer: For retryable side-effecting operations whose outcome may become uncertain, such as payment creation or order submission.

questions.question: Why must an idempotency key include an operation scope?
questions.answer: Keys must not collide across tenants or unrelated operations; also bind the key to a consistent request meaning.

questions.question: Why is caching completed responses insufficient for concurrent duplicates?
questions.answer: Two requests can execute before either response is cached. Use an atomic claim and durable operation state with recovery.

questions.question: How would you choose deduplication retention?
questions.answer: Cover the documented retry and redelivery horizon plus recovery needs; define behavior after expiry rather than implying indefinite duplicate protection.

groups.title: Retries and budgets
groups.mechanism: Retries repeat work and consume time plus dependency capacity. Retryability depends on operation semantics and uncertainty, not only error codes.
groups.tradeOff: Retries help transient failures while amplifying overload if unbounded or synchronized.
groups.verify: Count attempts under nested retries and verify total elapsed time stays within the caller's budget.

questions.question: Which failures are candidates for retry?
questions.answer: Transient failures on safely repeatable operations, subject to a bounded deadline and explicit policy; permanent validation and authorization failures usually are not.

questions.question: Why use backoff with jitter?
questions.answer: Backoff reduces repeated immediate pressure; jitter spreads synchronized clients so they do not all retry together.

questions.question: How do layered retries multiply work?
questions.answer: Each layer can repeat all downstream attempts. Three attempts at three layers can yield 27 final dependency calls.

questions.question: Why can a timeout be an ambiguous success?
questions.answer: The remote side may have committed before the response was lost or the caller stopped waiting.

questions.question: How would you implement a retry budget?
questions.answer: Limit extra attempts relative to useful traffic or capacity, preserve the overall deadline and measure both attempted calls and successful business effects.

groups.title: Circuit breakers and bulkheads
groups.mechanism: Circuit breakers limit attempts toward failing dependencies; bulkheads limit shared-resource contention. They solve different problems and need explicit recovery behavior.
groups.tradeOff: Isolation consumes capacity while protecting unrelated capabilities from shared exhaustion.
groups.verify: Fail one dependency and verify unrelated endpoints retain usable capacity.

questions.question: What does a circuit breaker do?
questions.answer: It changes admission toward a dependency according to failure and recovery policy, commonly rejecting calls temporarily after failures.

questions.question: When is a bulkhead useful?
questions.answer: When one dependency or workload can otherwise exhaust threads, connections or concurrency shared with unrelated work.

questions.question: How does half-open recovery differ from normal traffic?
questions.answer: It permits controlled probes to decide whether the dependency has recovered rather than immediately restoring full load.

questions.question: Why does a circuit breaker not replace a timeout?
questions.answer: A call already executing can still hang; per-call deadlines and cancellation ownership are separate from circuit admission state.

questions.question: How would you design a truthful fallback?
questions.answer: Return only a degraded result whose meaning is valid for that operation, with explicit freshness or uncertainty; never fabricate committed business success.

groups.title: Load balancing and discovery
groups.mechanism: Discovery supplies candidate endpoints; load balancing selects among them under health, locality and connection behavior. Removal is not instantaneous everywhere.
groups.tradeOff: Locality reduces latency but can concentrate risk or capacity pressure.
groups.verify: Drain an instance and inspect new requests, existing connections and stale discovery entries.

questions.question: What is service discovery?
questions.answer: A mechanism for locating current service instances or endpoints under an explicit naming and update model.

questions.question: When should client-side balancing be used?
questions.answer: When the client integration deliberately owns endpoint selection and health behavior; compare it with managed proxy or platform balancing.

questions.question: Why do persistent connections affect traffic distribution?
questions.answer: Several requests can share one selected connection, so request distribution may differ from simple endpoint-count assumptions.

questions.question: What happens when discovery information is stale?
questions.answer: Clients may contact removed or unhealthy instances until refresh, connection failure or retry policy changes their selection.

questions.question: How would you reduce deployment drain errors?
questions.answer: Withdraw readiness, account for discovery and routing propagation, bound old connections and allow a measured in-flight completion window.

groups.title: Caching and consistency
groups.mechanism: Caching creates another representation with its own freshness and failure semantics. Invalidation and concurrent loading must preserve the chosen business contract.
groups.tradeOff: Lower latency and origin load compete with stale reads and coordination cost.
groups.verify: Expire hot keys, update origin data and inject invalidation failure under concurrent reads.

questions.question: When is cache-aside appropriate?
questions.answer: When the application can tolerate an explicit staleness policy and owns cache lookup, origin loading and invalidation behavior.

questions.question: What is a cache stampede?
questions.answer: Many concurrent misses rebuild the same expensive value and overload the origin, often after synchronized expiry or cold deployment.

questions.question: How can stale-while-revalidate help?
questions.answer: It serves an allowed stale value while controlled refresh occurs, trading bounded freshness for reduced synchronous load.

questions.question: Why can invalidation before commit produce incorrect cache state?
questions.answer: A concurrent reader can reload old committed data before the write commits, leaving the cache stale after the transaction succeeds.

questions.question: How would you cache authorization-sensitive data?
questions.answer: Include all identity and policy dimensions affecting the value, limit stale authorization decisions and keep enforcement at the authoritative boundary.

groups.title: Sagas and compensation
groups.mechanism: A saga coordinates local transactions with explicit forward and compensating actions. Compensation is a business operation, not time travel or guaranteed rollback.
groups.tradeOff: Availability across independent services comes with intermediate states and recovery complexity.
groups.verify: Fail every step and each compensation, then verify durable progress and safe retries.

questions.question: What is a saga?
questions.answer: A sequence of local transactions coordinated with explicit recovery or compensation when the overall business process cannot complete normally.

questions.question: When is orchestration preferable to choreography?
questions.answer: When centralized process visibility and control outweigh coupling to a coordinator; choose from ownership, complexity and failure diagnosis needs.

questions.question: How does compensation differ from database rollback?
questions.answer: It performs a new business action after earlier effects became visible, and may be partial, delayed or impossible.

questions.question: Why can refunding fail after payment succeeds?
questions.answer: Compensation uses another external operation with its own availability and outcome ambiguity; persist and reconcile its state.

questions.question: How would you model an unrecoverable saga state?
questions.answer: Expose a durable pending or manual-resolution status, retain evidence and prevent uncontrolled retries from repeating irreversible effects.

groups.title: Transactional outbox
groups.mechanism: An outbox stores business change and publication intent in one local transaction. The relay can send before recording success, so duplicates remain possible.
groups.tradeOff: It closes a local atomicity gap while adding lag, storage and relay ownership.
groups.verify: Crash before commit, after commit and after send but before marking publication.

questions.question: What problem does the outbox pattern solve?
questions.answer: It avoids losing the intent to publish an event when a local database change commits but direct broker publication fails.

questions.question: When should a consumer inbox be added?
questions.answer: When duplicate events need durable detection or ordering before applying the consumer's local business effect.

questions.question: How can an outbox relay duplicate a message?
questions.answer: It may publish successfully and crash before recording that publication, then send again after restart.

questions.question: Why is deleting outbox entries immediately risky?
questions.answer: Deletion can remove evidence needed for replay, reconciliation or diagnosing ambiguous publication, depending on the recovery contract.

questions.question: How would you operate a high-volume outbox?
questions.answer: Bound batches, partition ownership, track lag and failures, index pending work and retain enough durable identity for duplicate-safe recovery.

groups.title: Event schema evolution
groups.mechanism: Events are durable contracts interpreted by present and future consumers. Field meaning, keys and replay behavior matter beyond schema compatibility tooling.
groups.tradeOff: Tolerant evolution reduces coordination but requires stable semantics and retained version knowledge.
groups.verify: Replay old events through new readers and new events through supported old consumers.

questions.question: How does an event differ from a command?
questions.answer: An event records something that happened; a command requests an action whose acceptance and completion still need a defined outcome.

questions.question: When is an additive event change safe?
questions.answer: When supported readers tolerate the addition and existing fields retain their meaning; schema acceptance alone does not establish behavioral compatibility.

questions.question: Why should an event include stable business identity?
questions.answer: Consumers need correlation, deduplication, ordering scope and reconciliation independent of transient transport delivery identifiers.

questions.question: What breaks when a historical field is silently reinterpreted?
questions.answer: Replay and older consumers can apply a different business meaning to the same stored data, corrupting derived state.

questions.question: How would you retire an event field?
questions.answer: Track consumers, preserve tolerant reading, migrate projections and only remove the field under an explicit compatibility and retention policy.

groups.title: Ordering and delivery
groups.mechanism: Delivery guarantees apply within a defined transport and processing scope. Business effects require their own durable identity and completion model.
groups.tradeOff: Stronger ordering simplifies reasoning while reducing parallelism within the ordered scope.
groups.verify: Redeliver messages out of order and restart between effect and acknowledgment.

questions.question: What does at-least-once delivery imply?
questions.answer: A record may be delivered again, so consumers must tolerate duplicates and distinguish delivery from committed business completion.

questions.question: When is per-entity ordering sufficient?
questions.answer: When invariants depend only on one aggregate or key, allowing unrelated entities to progress independently.

questions.question: Why is global ordering expensive?
questions.answer: It restricts parallelism and requires coordination across otherwise independent producers or partitions.

questions.question: How can acknowledgment before processing lose work?
questions.answer: Progress can become durable while the business effect is unfinished; after restart the transport may not redeliver that work.

questions.question: How would you handle out-of-order updates?
questions.answer: Use domain versions or sequence rules, reject stale writes and define recovery for gaps rather than trusting arrival time.

groups.title: Consistency and replication
groups.mechanism: Consistency describes observable ordering and visibility, while replication and availability describe different dimensions. A replicated service can still expose stale data.
groups.tradeOff: Stronger guarantees can require coordination that affects latency or availability during failures.
groups.verify: Read after writes through different replicas and inject network delay or partition.

questions.question: What is eventual consistency?
questions.answer: Replicas or derived views converge under stated assumptions after updates stop and replication succeeds, without promising immediate identical reads.

questions.question: When does read-your-writes matter?
questions.answer: When a user expects an acknowledged change to be visible in subsequent interactions, such as profile edits or order status.

questions.question: How does a network partition affect consistency choices?
questions.answer: Some operations must reject or delay rather than serve conflicting states if their consistency guarantee is to be preserved.

questions.question: Why is a quorum not a universal linearizability guarantee?
questions.answer: Correctness depends on membership, write/read protocols, failure handling and overlapping operation ordering, not merely counting responses.

questions.question: How would you choose a consistency model for inventory?
questions.answer: State the overselling invariant, select authoritative atomic operations and define what availability or latency may be sacrificed during uncertainty.

groups.title: Authentication and authorization
groups.mechanism: Identity trust, service identity and resource authorization are separate controls. Network location alone does not establish who may act for which user.
groups.tradeOff: Central policy simplifies management but services still own business authorization boundaries.
groups.verify: Test wrong tenant, expired credentials and service-to-service calls without user permission.

questions.question: How do user identity and workload identity differ?
questions.answer: One identifies the person or caller principal; the other identifies the executing service. Delegation requires a separate explicit trust contract.

questions.question: When should a service validate a token independently?
questions.answer: When it is an enforcement boundary; do not blindly trust arbitrary forwarded identity headers from untrusted request paths.

questions.question: What does least privilege mean between services?
questions.answer: Each workload receives only the actions and resources required for its role, with controlled credential lifetime and auditable use.

questions.question: Why is a valid role insufficient for object access?
questions.answer: The requested object may belong to another tenant or owner; enforce resource-level conditions alongside role checks.

questions.question: How would you rotate service credentials safely?
questions.answer: Use overlapping trusted versions where supported, short-lived identities, observable refresh failures and a tested removal schedule.

groups.title: Observability
groups.mechanism: Logs, metrics and traces answer related but different questions. Useful correlations preserve causality through asynchronous and retried work without leaking sensitive data.
groups.tradeOff: High-detail telemetry adds storage, cardinality and runtime cost.
groups.verify: Trace one operation across retries and events, then confirm every business effect has a durable correlation.

questions.question: What does distributed tracing reveal?
questions.answer: The causal timing of instrumented operations across boundaries, helping separate local execution, queueing and dependency waits.

questions.question: When should a metric label be avoided?
questions.answer: When it has unbounded values such as raw user IDs, request IDs or arbitrary URLs, which can overwhelm the metrics system.

questions.question: How does trace context differ from business operation identity?
questions.answer: Trace context describes one diagnostic execution chain; operation identity may need to survive retries, replays and longer business workflows.

questions.question: Why can averaging latency conceal a regression?
questions.answer: A small but important slow population can violate tail targets while the overall average changes little.

questions.question: How would you define useful service-level indicators?
questions.answer: Measure user-visible successful outcomes and latency with clear denominators, exclusions and error classification rather than only process uptime.

groups.title: Deployment compatibility
groups.mechanism: Rolling releases temporarily run multiple versions against shared protocols and data. Backward-compatible writes and readers are essential for safe rollback.
groups.tradeOff: Gradual rollout reduces exposure but adds mixed-version states to test.
groups.verify: Run old and new instances concurrently against the expanded schema and event contracts.

questions.question: What is a canary deployment?
questions.answer: A limited rollout evaluated against explicit health and business criteria before wider traffic or instance expansion.

questions.question: When is blue-green deployment useful?
questions.answer: When switching between prepared environments simplifies release and rollback, while shared database and external-effect compatibility remain addressed.

questions.question: How does expand-contract schema migration work?
questions.answer: Add compatible structures first, migrate readers and writers, backfill, and only then remove old structures after consumers permit it.

questions.question: Why can routing rollback fail to restore service?
questions.answer: The new version may have written incompatible data or emitted events that old code cannot interpret.

questions.question: How would you set rollout stop conditions?
questions.answer: Define error, latency, saturation and business-invariant thresholds before deployment, with enough comparable baseline traffic to detect meaningful changes.

groups.title: Capacity and backpressure
groups.mechanism: Queues store outstanding demand; they do not create service capacity. Admission control decides which work is accepted before deadlines or memory become impossible.
groups.tradeOff: Rejecting early sacrifices some requests while protecting useful throughput and recovery.
groups.verify: Overload the system and confirm bounded memory, queue age and downstream concurrency.

questions.question: What is backpressure?
questions.answer: A mechanism for aligning production or admission with consumer capacity, rather than letting pending work grow without bound.

questions.question: When should a request be rejected immediately?
questions.answer: When capacity or remaining deadline makes useful completion unlikely and the contract supports a truthful retryable rejection.

questions.question: How does Little's Law guide capacity reasoning?
questions.answer: In a stable system, average outstanding work relates to throughput and average time in system; use consistent boundaries and units.

questions.question: Why can autoscaling fail to relieve a database bottleneck?
questions.answer: More application instances can multiply connections and offered load while the shared database's processing capacity stays fixed.

questions.question: How would you design overload recovery?
questions.answer: Bound admission and queues, prioritize useful work, prevent retry storms and restore traffic gradually as dependency capacity becomes available.

groups.title: Multi-tenancy
groups.mechanism: Tenant identity must be carried through authorization, data access, caching and telemetry. Isolation is a system-wide invariant rather than one request filter.
groups.tradeOff: Stronger separation increases operational cost but limits cross-tenant failure and exposure.
groups.verify: Run concurrent tenants with identical resource IDs and conflicting load patterns.

questions.question: What are common tenant isolation strategies?
questions.answer: Shared tables with tenant keys, separate schemas or separate databases, chosen according to security, scaling and operational requirements.

questions.question: When should tenant identity be resolved?
questions.answer: At a trusted boundary from authenticated context, then validated and carried explicitly through downstream decisions.

questions.question: How can a cache leak tenant data?
questions.answer: A key that omits tenant identity can reuse another tenant's result even when the underlying database queries were correctly scoped.

questions.question: Why can one tenant starve others despite correct data isolation?
questions.answer: Shared pools, queues and rate limits may allow noisy-neighbor resource exhaustion without per-tenant admission controls.

questions.question: How would you test tenant isolation end to end?
questions.answer: Use overlapping IDs, concurrent requests, async jobs and cached results; assert both authorization outcomes and bounded cross-tenant resource impact.

groups.title: Incident recovery and reconciliation
groups.mechanism: A distributed incident can leave partially completed business operations. Recovery must establish durable truth before repeating uncertain effects.
groups.tradeOff: Fast restoration competes with evidence preservation and the risk of duplicate actions.
groups.verify: Inject failure at every commit/response boundary and exercise the documented reconciliation workflow.

questions.question: What is reconciliation in distributed systems?
questions.answer: Comparing durable records across components to detect and resolve missing, duplicated or inconsistent business outcomes.

questions.question: When should operators avoid blindly replaying failed requests?
questions.answer: When a timeout or lost response leaves the original effect uncertain and repeating it could duplicate an irreversible action.

questions.question: How do recovery point and recovery time objectives differ?
questions.answer: RPO concerns acceptable data loss; RTO concerns acceptable restoration time. Both must be tied to tested recovery capabilities.

questions.question: Why is restoring a backup insufficient evidence of full recovery?
questions.answer: Clients, event offsets, external effects and derived views may remain inconsistent with the restored database state.

questions.question: How would you close a distributed incident safely?
questions.answer: Restore capacity, reconcile ambiguous operations, verify business invariants and add targeted regression plus operational evidence for the actual failure window.

groups.title: API Gateway and Backend for Frontend patterns
groups.mechanism: A gateway centralizes selected transport concerns; a BFF shapes APIs for a particular client experience. Neither should become an uncontrolled shared domain monolith.
groups.tradeOff: Centralization simplifies clients while increasing shared blast radius and ownership coupling.
groups.verify: Fail the gateway's optional dependencies and verify unrelated client capabilities retain defined behavior.

questions.question: What is the API Gateway pattern?
questions.answer: A controlled entry point providing selected routing, authentication, limits or aggregation in front of services under an explicit contract.

questions.question: When is a Backend for Frontend useful?
questions.answer: When different clients have substantially different composition or representation needs that justify separately owned adaptation layers.

questions.question: How should authorization be split across gateway and service?
questions.answer: The gateway can enforce edge policy, while services still enforce trusted identity and resource-specific business authorization.

questions.question: Why can a gateway become a bottleneck organizationally?
questions.answer: Every domain change may require a shared team and release if too much business logic is centralized there.

questions.question: How would you keep gateway aggregation resilient?
questions.answer: Bound fan-out, distinguish required and optional data, propagate deadlines and return truthful partial results without duplicating domain ownership.

groups.title: CQRS and materialized views
groups.mechanism: CQRS separates write and read models where their needs differ. Asynchronous projections introduce lag and rebuild concerns; CQRS does not require event sourcing.
groups.tradeOff: Read optimization adds operational complexity and consistency decisions.
groups.verify: Rebuild projections from authoritative history and test read-after-write behavior during lag.

questions.question: What is CQRS?
questions.answer: Separating command-side changes from query-side models when different responsibilities or performance needs justify distinct representations.

questions.question: When is CQRS unnecessary?
questions.answer: When one straightforward transactional model already serves reads and writes adequately and separate projections add no meaningful benefit.

questions.question: How can a projection recover after an outage?
questions.answer: Replay or reconcile from a retained authoritative source with durable checkpoints, duplicate handling and versioned transformation logic.

questions.question: Why can a command succeed while the query result stays old?
questions.answer: The write committed before asynchronous projection processing caught up; the API needs an explicit visibility contract.

questions.question: How would you evolve a materialized view?
questions.answer: Version the projection logic, backfill or replay safely, compare results and cut over readers with rollback plus freshness monitoring.

groups.title: Event sourcing pattern
groups.mechanism: Event sourcing stores an authoritative event history from which current state is derived. Event evolution and replay safety become core data-management responsibilities.
groups.tradeOff: Auditability and temporal reconstruction compete with schema, privacy and operational complexity.
groups.verify: Replay historical streams with new code and verify deterministic state plus rejected invalid transitions.

questions.question: What distinguishes event sourcing from publishing integration events?
questions.answer: Event history is the authoritative persisted state, rather than a secondary notification emitted from a separate current-state database.

questions.question: When is event sourcing worth considering?
questions.answer: When durable history and reconstruction materially serve the domain and the team can own event evolution, replay and operational complexity.

questions.question: How do snapshots help event-sourced aggregates?
questions.answer: They provide a supported state checkpoint to reduce replay work, while retained events and version compatibility remain necessary.

questions.question: Why must replay avoid ordinary external side effects?
questions.answer: Rebuilding state must not charge, email or publish the same business action again merely because historical events are reprocessed.

questions.question: How would you handle an incorrect historical event?
questions.answer: Preserve the audit contract and apply explicit corrective events or controlled migration; do not silently rewrite history without a defined governance policy.

groups.title: Strangler Fig migration pattern
groups.mechanism: The strangler pattern replaces legacy capabilities incrementally behind controlled routing or boundaries. Shared data and mixed ownership require explicit transitional rules.
groups.tradeOff: Incremental delivery reduces cutover risk while prolonging temporary integration complexity.
groups.verify: Route selected operations to each implementation and verify shared invariants under mixed versions.

questions.question: What is the Strangler Fig pattern?
questions.answer: Incrementally replacing legacy functionality by routing selected capabilities to new implementations while retiring old paths over time.

questions.question: When is an anti-corruption layer useful during migration?
questions.answer: When translating legacy terminology and behavior prevents the new domain model from inheriting incompatible assumptions.

questions.question: How can routing by operation support gradual migration?
questions.answer: It allows a bounded capability to move while other operations retain the existing implementation, with explicit ownership and rollback criteria.

questions.question: Why is dual writing without a recovery protocol dangerous?
questions.answer: One write can succeed while the other fails, creating divergent authoritative states and ambiguous repair decisions.

questions.question: How would you migrate data ownership incrementally?
questions.answer: Choose one authority per phase, replicate or reconcile explicitly, verify cutover consistency and prevent old writers from continuing after ownership changes.

groups.title: Sidecar and service mesh patterns
groups.mechanism: A sidecar or mesh can provide selected communication capabilities near workloads. It cannot infer domain idempotency or resource-level business authorization.
groups.tradeOff: Shared infrastructure policy reduces repetition while adding another failure and upgrade surface.
groups.verify: Observe behavior with proxy delay, restart and policy mismatch while tracing actual attempted calls.

questions.question: What is the sidecar pattern?
questions.answer: Deploying a cooperating helper alongside a workload to provide a focused capability with an explicit lifecycle and communication contract.

questions.question: When can a service mesh help?
questions.answer: When consistent workload communication policy, transport identity or telemetry justifies the added operational and debugging complexity.

questions.question: Does a mesh retry make every operation safe?
questions.answer: No. Transport retries can duplicate committed business effects unless the application operation has a safe idempotency contract.

questions.question: Why can application and mesh retries amplify load?
questions.answer: Both layers may repeat requests independently, multiplying attempts beyond the intended budget.

questions.question: How would you adopt mesh policies safely?
questions.answer: Inventory existing application behavior, define one owner for retry/deadline policy and test failure plus rollout interactions before broad enforcement.

groups.title: Pattern selection and composition
groups.mechanism: Patterns protect particular invariants under stated assumptions. Combining patterns can change ordering, capacity and failure semantics, so composition needs end-to-end evidence.
groups.tradeOff: More patterns can add failure modes without improving the actual requirement.
groups.verify: Trace one operation through every pattern and inject failure between each durable boundary.

questions.question: How would you choose a microservices pattern?
questions.answer: Start with a concrete problem and invariant, compare simpler alternatives and select the smallest pattern whose assumptions fit.

questions.question: When should a proposed service be merged back?
questions.answer: When coordination, latency and change coupling consistently exceed the benefit of independent deployment or ownership.

questions.question: How do outbox, inbox and saga complement each other?
questions.answer: Outbox preserves publication intent, inbox can protect consumer effects, and saga coordinates longer business progress with explicit recovery.

questions.question: Why does combining reliable components not guarantee a reliable workflow?
questions.answer: Their completion boundaries and assumptions may not align, leaving gaps between commits, acknowledgments and external effects.

questions.question: How would you defend a design in an interview?
questions.answer: Name the invariant, explain one realistic failure path, justify the trade-off and describe a test that would falsify your correctness claim.
